title: Decidability of termination for one-rule string rewriting
formal: Is global termination of a one-rule string rewriting system decidable? The input is a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) and two explicitly written words \(\ell,r\in\Sigma^{*}\). Define \(u\to v\) when \(u=x\ell y\) and \(v=xry\) for some \(x,y\in\Sigma^{*}\). Decide whether there exists no infinite sequence \(w_0\to w_1\to w_2\to\cdots\) of finite words. The quantifier includes every starting word and every choice of replacement position.
why: A single literal replacement is among the simplest possible descriptions of an unbounded computation. Settling its global termination problem would locate a sharp limit on automatic reasoning about repeated symbolic transformations, without relying on a large instruction set or richer term syntax.
status_note: The 2002 primary paper and the August 2026 authored note present arbitrary one-rule termination as unresolved. A bounded check on 13 September 2026 found no later resolution. The note and historical proofs have not been independently verified; source-open status is not an exhaustive certification.
review_note: Completed individual source and formulation review on 13 September 2026; see statement_review and research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

sentences: A one-rule string system repeatedly replaces one fixed substring by another.
The question is whether an algorithm can decide if every reduction sequence from every finite starting word eventually stops.
Replacement positions are unrestricted, and the rule and alphabet are part of the input.
Known decision procedures cover special rule families, while an August 2026 note still lists the arbitrary one-rule question as open.
The answer must prove decidability or undecidability in Lean for global termination, rather than only termination from one supplied word.

definitions: The alphabet is a finite nonempty set listed by distinct binary symbol indices. Both sides of the rule are explicit finite sequences of these symbols, including possibly the empty word \(\varepsilon\). No variables, compressed word descriptions, contexts supplied as inputs, or additional rewrite rules occur.

One rewrite step chooses one contiguous occurrence of \(\ell\) and replaces it with \(r\), preserving the prefix \(x\) and suffix \(y\). If \(\ell=\varepsilon\), any boundary in a word, including its ends, is an occurrence. A rule application counts as a step even when the resulting word is identical to the original word. Thus \(\ell=r\) admits a constant infinite reduction sequence from \(\ell\).

Global termination means that for every \(w_0\in\Sigma^{*}\) there is no function \(w:\mathbb{N}\to\Sigma^{*}\) with first value \(w_0\) and \(w_i\to w_{i+1}\) for all \(i\geq0\). There is no fixed leftmost or rightmost evaluation strategy. Requiring only that each word has some terminating sequence would be a different property.

Decidability asks for a single deterministic Turing machine that halts on every valid finite description and outputs yes exactly for globally terminating systems. No running-time bound is imposed. Malformed descriptions can be rejected. The rule itself varies across instances; neither its length nor the alphabet size is a fixed constant.
answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of a total decision algorithm for all one-rule systems in this model, or a Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists. Deciding termination from one supplied start word, analyzing one strategy, or handling a restricted family of rules alone is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: Geser’s paper gives decidability for grid rules: there is a letter \(b\) occurring on the left whose count on the right is no larger. It explicitly distinguishes this substantial subclass from the unresolved arbitrary one-rule problem.
RTA Problem 21 distinguishes the string case from the more general question for a single linear term-rewriting rule. This card asks only about replacements of contiguous substrings.
Kfoury’s August 2026 note restates global one-rule termination as Open Problem 8. It is a source-status update, rather than a new proof of either answer.

statement_review.notes: Expanded the saved global-termination question without changing its target. Defined arbitrary replacement positions, all starting words and reduction sequences, empty rules and self-steps, explicit alphabet/word encoding and one uniform terminating decision machine. Recovered the original reference metadata and distinguished string rewriting from the separate linear-term question.
